nameStory: The lumpfish gets its name from its distinctly lumpy, bumpy appearance - it looks like nature sculpted a fish out of rocky terrain! The 'sucker' part of its alternate name 'lumpsucker' comes from its amazing ability to stick to rocks and surfaces using a specialized sucker disc on its belly.
description: The lumpfish is a chunky, round-bodied marine fish that looks almost prehistoric with its bumpy, warty skin covered in rows of bony tubercles (small round bumps). Adults can grow quite large, reaching up to 2 feet long, with thick, gelatinous flesh that feels surprisingly soft despite their armored appearance. They're most famous for their powerful sucker disc on their underside, which lets them cling tightly to rocks in turbulent waters. These hardy fish are built for cold northern waters and have a distinctive humpbacked profile that makes them unmistakable.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly round and chunky with a pronounced hump behind the head, feeling thick and gelatinous to the touch with surprisingly soft, almost jelly-like flesh beneath bumpy skin

idTips.label: Skin Texture
idTips.description: Covered in rows of hard, bony bumps called tubercles that feel like small pebbles embedded in thick, slimy skin - no scales like typical fish

idTips.label: Sucker Disc
idTips.description: Large, circular sucker on the belly formed from modified pelvic fins that feels like a rubber suction cup and can grip surfaces with surprising strength

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Usually mottled gray, brown, or greenish with darker blotches that help camouflage against rocky bottoms, though breeding males can turn bright orange or red

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Small fins relative to body size, with the first dorsal fin often appearing as just a ridge of bumps, and pelvic fins completely modified into the sucker disc

habitat: Lumpfish live in cold New England coastal waters, typically found clinging to rocky bottoms, kelp forests, and pier pilings from shallow tide pools down to deeper offshore waters. They prefer areas with strong currents where their sucker disc gives them a major advantage over other fish. You're most likely to spot them during low tide attached to rocks in the intertidal zone or occasionally washed up after storms.

seasonality.spring: Spawning season begins as adults move into shallower coastal waters. Males develop bright breeding colors and can be found guarding nests attached to rocks.
seasonality.summer: Peak spawning continues with males turning vivid orange or red while tending egg masses. Best time to observe them in shallow waters and tide pools.
seasonality.fall: Adults begin moving to deeper waters as water temperatures drop. Juvenile lumpfish may still be found in shallow areas.
seasonality.winter: Adults retreat to deeper offshore waters. Rarely seen in shallow areas except occasionally after winter storms.

funFact: Male lumpfish are devoted dads who turn bright orange during breeding season and literally glue themselves to rocks next to their eggs for up to two months, barely eating while they fan and guard their babies - some males actually starve themselves to death protecting their offspring!
confusionNotes: Could be mistaken for a sea robin due to similar bottom-dwelling habits, but lumpfish have that unmistakable sucker disc on their belly and much bumpier skin. Remember: if it sticks like glue to rocks and feels like a bumpy water balloon, it's a lumpfish!
contextualKnowledge: Despite their odd appearance, lumpfish are commercially important - their eggs are harvested as a caviar substitute, and the fish themselves are used as 'cleaner fish' in salmon farms to eat sea lice off the salmon. They're also sometimes called 'henfish' in some New England fishing communities.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus Cyclopterus, lumpfish are easily distinguished from other lumpsucker family members by their much larger size and more pronounced tubercles. Other cyclopterids in New England waters are much smaller and smoother, lacking the dramatic bumpy armor and powerful sucker disc of the true lumpfish.
